bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Market leadership in North-East India built over more than two decades of presence, with an approximately 25% trade market share in FY26 and the first cement brand in the region to surpass 5 MTPA of sales in a single financial year.
- Distribution depth — a network of 1,850+ dealers and 11,200+ retailers (RSARs) giving last-mile reach across Eastern and North-Eastern India, reinforced by three digital loyalty platforms (Star Saathi, Star Link, Star Stellar).
- Integrated, cost-efficient manufacturing at Lumshnong with captive limestone reserves, a 51 MW captive thermal power plant and a 24.3 MW Waste Heat Recovery System, and clinker sourced power supplied under a long-term arrangement from wholly owned subsidiary Star Cement Meghalaya Limited.
- Logistics as a competitive advantage in difficult North-East terrain — a dedicated fleet including 274 16-wheelers for clinker movement from Lumshnong to the Guwahati grinding units, weighted average lead distance reduced from 225 km to 221 km and the rail coefficient improved from 6% to 12%.
- Brand equity and premiumisation — Star Weather Shield and Star Dhalai Master raised premium products to about 14% of trade sales in FY 25-26 from about 11% in FY 24-25.
- Energy and cost flexibility — renewable energy usage of approximately 33-35%, open access power procurement through IEX (DAM, RTM and GDAM) at rates below prevailing DISCOM tariffs, and a long-term Fuel Supply Agreement with Coal India Limited.
- Long-term raw material security from captive limestone reserves plus preferred-bidder status for the Parewar (SN-IV) limestone mine in Jaisalmer, Rajasthan with estimated reserves of 271.38 million tonnes.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Industry-wide capacity addition and intensifying competition — The Board's Report and MD&A record that FY 2025-26 marked a phase of accelerated capacity expansion across the industry, with major cement manufacturers undertaking both greenfield and brownfield projects to enhance production capabilities and strengthen regional presence. Rising supply raises the risk of competitive pricing pressure in the Company's core and adjacent markets.
- Dependence on government-led capital expenditure for demand — Management states that demand momentum remained largely driven by government-led capital expenditure programmes, expansion of transport infrastructure and ongoing urban and rural development initiatives. Cement offtake is therefore exposed to any slowdown or reprioritisation of public infrastructure and affordable housing spending.
- End-market concentration in housing and infrastructure — The housing and infrastructure segments remained the primary contributors to cement consumption, collectively accounting for a substantial share of overall demand, leaving volumes tied to the construction cycle in those two segments.
- Energy cost and carbon intensity exposure in an energy-intensive process — Operations remain energy-intensive — specific thermal energy consumption of 700.1 kcal/kg of clinker and specific power consumption of 31.2 kWh/tonne of cement — with renewable and WHRS sources at 33.3% of the energy mix, so the majority of energy needs are still met from conventional sources whose cost and carbon intensity the Company is actively working to reduce through WHRS, variable frequency drives, energy-efficient motors and automated energy management.
- Concentration of leadership in the promoter group with an extensive related-party network — During FY 25-26 the Board comprised 15 Directors including 8 Independent Directors and 2 Women Directors, with the promoter family holding the Chairman, Managing Director and MD & CEO positions and several directors also serving on boards of related entities. The Company reports the separation of the Chairman and MD & CEO roles during the year, a six-committee framework including a Risk Management Committee, and a Whistle Blower and Vigil Mechanism as mitigants, and reports no related-party governance concerns, regulatory penalties or sexual harassment complaints for the year.
- Execution and transition risk in cleaner-operations initiatives — The Company is only at pilot stage in deploying electric vehicles for on-site material movement in mining operations, with broader adoption explicitly dependent on the supporting ecosystem maturing — a decarbonisation pathway whose timing is outside the Company's control.
- Community and social licence dependence around plant locations — Operations are concentrated around the Lumshnong plant and neighbouring villages, where the Company sustains its social licence through CSR spending across 19 villages, 54 community development projects, health camps, education support and rural infrastructure — a dependence that makes community relations material to uninterrupted operations.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY 25-26 was a capacity-addition year. The Company's wholly owned subsidiary Star Cement North East Limited commissioned a 2 MTPA grinding unit in the Cachar area of Silchar district, Assam on 20 February 2026, taking total grinding capacity to 9.7 MTPA (cement capacity of 9.67 MTPA against 6.1 MTPA of clinker capacity). The railway siding at the Silchar grinding unit is progressing at a fast pace and is expected to be operational by Q3 FY27, strengthening logistics efficiency and reducing transportation costs. Star Cement North East Limited has also been declared preferred bidder for the limestone mine at Parewar (SN-IV), District Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, with estimated reserves of 271.38 million tonnes, securing long-term raw material for expansion into new markets. A pipeline of projects is under implementation: a 2 MTPA grinding unit in Bihar, planned as a natural extension of the Siliguri grinding unit and expected to be commissioned by FY28 with the support of government incentives; and two greenfield projects in North India — a 3.3 MTPA clinker unit together with a 2.5 MTPA grinding unit at Nimbol, Rajasthan, and a 2 MTPA grinding unit at Jhajjar, Haryana — both expected to be commissioned by FY28. Management states it is scaling installed cement capacity to 15 MTPA by the end of FY29, consistent with the stated vision of reaching 15 million metric tonnes of manufacturing capacity over the next five years. In the Other Building Materials segment, subsidiary Star Smart Building Solutions Limited commissioned an 800 cubic metre Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (AAC) block plant on 2 June 2025 at Chamata Pathar, Sonapur, adjacent to the existing grinding unit near Guwahati, and the Company extended into construction chemicals including wall putty and entered Ready-Mix Concrete with intent to scale in phases. Earlier milestones in the capacity build include the FY 24-25 commissioning of a 3.3 MTPA clinker line plus an additional 12 MW Waste Heat Recovery System at Lumshnong, the FY 23-24 commissioning of a 2.0 MTPA grinding unit at Sonapur, Guwahati, the FY 22-23 commissioning of a 12.3 MW WHRS at Lumshnong and the FY 20-21 commissioning of a 2.0 MTPA grinding unit at Mohitnagar, Siliguri. Star Cement reports 5 manufacturing facilities: 1 integrated manufacturing unit with WHR, 3 cement grinding units, 1 clinker unit with cement grinding and a 51 MW captive thermal power plant and WHR, and 1 AAC block facility. Debottlenecking of clinker lines and the ramp-up of the expanded Guwahati Grinding Unit and Line-III clinker capacity were the other capacity levers during the year. Of the Company's capex investments in FY 2025-26, 7.73% went to specific technologies improving environmental and social impacts (against 23% in FY 2024-25), covering environmental monitoring equipment, a first aid room and fly ash construction. The rupee quantum of total capital expenditure is not stated in usable form in this bundle.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Cement demand in India recorded mid-single-digit growth in FY 2025-26, driven by government-led capital expenditure, transport infrastructure expansion and urban and rural development initiatives.
- Housing and infrastructure remained the primary contributors to cement consumption, supported by affordable housing, highway and rail network expansion and industrial and logistics infrastructure.
- The North-East regional market is sized at approximately 13 MMT and growing at 8-10%, and remains structurally underpenetrated — India's per capita cement consumption of 290-340 kg is well below the global average of 470-520 kg, with the North East lagging even the national mean.
- Sustained government capex under PM-DevINE and other North East-focused infrastructure programmes, improving rural incomes and accelerating urbanisation are expected to support above-industry volume growth for the Company through this cycle.
- Industry production is forecast to sustain momentum in FY27 with 7-8% growth, underpinned by housing and infrastructure demand.
- Average cement prices rose approximately 2% year-on-year to Rs 345/bag in FY26 and are projected to increase a further 2-4% in FY27, supported by healthy demand and improved pricing discipline.
- ICRA estimates industry PBITDA/MT will rise to Rs 900-950 in FY26 before moderating to Rs 820-870 per MT in FY27, reflecting anticipated headwinds from fuel and freight cost inflation.
- The industry is entering a major capacity expansion cycle — CRISIL projects 150-160 MT of new capacity between FY25 and FY28 — which is expected to intensify competitive dynamics and require disciplined pricing and efficient cost management.
- Policy tailwinds: the Union Budget 2026-27 allocates a record Rs 12.2 lakh crore to capital expenditure, with Rs 3.09 lakh crore to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, alongside PM Gati Shakti, PMAY-Urban 2.0, AMRUT and Smart Cities, Bharatmala and Sagarmala, and Jal Jeevan Mission.
- Geopolitical tension between the United States and Iran could push crude and gas prices upward; higher diesel and pet-coke prices may exert pressure on operating margins given energy and freight are a significant share of cement production and distribution cost.
- Cost levers management is pulling: renewable energy usage of approximately 33-35%, WHRB captive generation, open-access power procurement through IEX at rates below DISCOM tariffs, biomass and bamboo as alternative fuels, and a long-term Fuel Supply Agreement with Coal India Limited.
- Logistics cost efficiency through e-bidding, PTPK outlier correction and wheeler- and segment-wise freight strategies reduced the weighted average lead distance from 225 km to 221 km and lifted the rail coefficient from 6% to 12%; the first cement barge dispatch via Hatsingimari in August 2025 opened inland waterway corridors.

currentContext.expansion: FY 25-26 was a capacity-addition year. The Company's wholly owned subsidiary Star Cement North East Limited commissioned a 2 MTPA grinding unit in the Cachar area of Silchar district, Assam on 20 February 2026, taking total grinding capacity to 9.7 MTPA (cement capacity of 9.67 MTPA against 6.1 MTPA of clinker capacity). The railway siding at the Silchar grinding unit is progressing at a fast pace and is expected to be operational by Q3 FY27, strengthening logistics efficiency and reducing transportation costs. Star Cement North East Limited has also been declared preferred bidder for the limestone mine at Parewar (SN-IV), District Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, with estimated reserves of 271.38 million tonnes, securing long-term raw material for expansion into new markets. A pipeline of projects is under implementation: a 2 MTPA grinding unit in Bihar, planned as a natural extension of the Siliguri grinding unit and expected to be commissioned by FY28 with the support of government incentives; and two greenfield projects in North India — a 3.3 MTPA clinker unit together with a 2.5 MTPA grinding unit at Nimbol, Rajasthan, and a 2 MTPA grinding unit at Jhajjar, Haryana — both expected to be commissioned by FY28. Management states it is scaling installed cement capacity to 15 MTPA by the end of FY29, consistent with the stated vision of reaching 15 million metric tonnes of manufacturing capacity over the next five years. In the Other Building Materials segment, subsidiary Star Smart Building Solutions Limited commissioned an 800 cubic metre Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (AAC) block plant on 2 June 2025 at Chamata Pathar, Sonapur, adjacent to the existing grinding unit near Guwahati, and the Company extended into construction chemicals including wall putty and entered Ready-Mix Concrete with intent to scale in phases. Earlier milestones in the capacity build include the FY 24-25 commissioning of a 3.3 MTPA clinker line plus an additional 12 MW Waste Heat Recovery System at Lumshnong, the FY 23-24 commissioning of a 2.0 MTPA grinding unit at Sonapur, Guwahati, the FY 22-23 commissioning of a 12.3 MW WHRS at Lumshnong and the FY 20-21 commissioning of a 2.0 MTPA grinding unit at Mohitnagar, Siliguri. Star Cement reports 5 manufacturing facilities: 1 integrated manufacturing unit with WHR, 3 cement grinding units, 1 clinker unit with cement grinding and a 51 MW captive thermal power plant and WHR, and 1 AAC block facility. Debottlenecking of clinker lines and the ramp-up of the expanded Guwahati Grinding Unit and Line-III clinker capacity were the other capacity levers during the year. Of the Company's capex investments in FY 2025-26, 7.73% went to specific technologies improving environmental and social impacts (against 23% in FY 2024-25), covering environmental monitoring equipment, a first aid room and fly ash construction. The rupee quantum of total capital expenditure is not stated in usable form in this bundle.

risks.risk: Industry-wide capacity addition and intensifying competition
risks.note: The Board's Report and MD&A record that FY 2025-26 marked a phase of accelerated capacity expansion across the industry, with major cement manufacturers undertaking both greenfield and brownfield projects to enhance production capabilities and strengthen regional presence. Rising supply raises the risk of competitive pricing pressure in the Company's core and adjacent markets.

risks.risk: Dependence on government-led capital expenditure for demand
risks.note: Management states that demand momentum remained largely driven by government-led capital expenditure programmes, expansion of transport infrastructure and ongoing urban and rural development initiatives. Cement offtake is therefore exposed to any slowdown or reprioritisation of public infrastructure and affordable housing spending.

risks.risk: End-market concentration in housing and infrastructure
risks.note: The housing and infrastructure segments remained the primary contributors to cement consumption, collectively accounting for a substantial share of overall demand, leaving volumes tied to the construction cycle in those two segments.

risks.risk: Energy cost and carbon intensity exposure in an energy-intensive process
risks.note: Operations remain energy-intensive — specific thermal energy consumption of 700.1 kcal/kg of clinker and specific power consumption of 31.2 kWh/tonne of cement — with renewable and WHRS sources at 33.3% of the energy mix, so the majority of energy needs are still met from conventional sources whose cost and carbon intensity the Company is actively working to reduce through WHRS, variable frequency drives, energy-efficient motors and automated energy management.

risks.risk: Concentration of leadership in the promoter group with an extensive related-party network
risks.note: During FY 25-26 the Board comprised 15 Directors including 8 Independent Directors and 2 Women Directors, with the promoter family holding the Chairman, Managing Director and MD & CEO positions and several directors also serving on boards of related entities. The Company reports the separation of the Chairman and MD & CEO roles during the year, a six-committee framework including a Risk Management Committee, and a Whistle Blower and Vigil Mechanism as mitigants, and reports no related-party governance concerns, regulatory penalties or sexual harassment complaints for the year.

risks.risk: Execution and transition risk in cleaner-operations initiatives
risks.note: The Company is only at pilot stage in deploying electric vehicles for on-site material movement in mining operations, with broader adoption explicitly dependent on the supporting ecosystem maturing — a decarbonisation pathway whose timing is outside the Company's control.

risks.risk: Community and social licence dependence around plant locations
risks.note: Operations are concentrated around the Lumshnong plant and neighbouring villages, where the Company sustains its social licence through CSR spending across 19 villages, 54 community development projects, health camps, education support and rural infrastructure — a dependence that makes community relations material to uninterrupted operations.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Cement demand in India recorded mid-single-digit growth in FY 2025-26, driven by government-led capital expenditure, transport infrastructure expansion and urban and rural development initiatives.
- Housing and infrastructure remained the primary contributors to cement consumption, supported by affordable housing, highway and rail network expansion and industrial and logistics infrastructure.
- The North-East regional market is sized at approximately 13 MMT and growing at 8-10%, and remains structurally underpenetrated — India's per capita cement consumption of 290-340 kg is well below the global average of 470-520 kg, with the North East lagging even the national mean.
- Sustained government capex under PM-DevINE and other North East-focused infrastructure programmes, improving rural incomes and accelerating urbanisation are expected to support above-industry volume growth for the Company through this cycle.
- Industry production is forecast to sustain momentum in FY27 with 7-8% growth, underpinned by housing and infrastructure demand.
- Average cement prices rose approximately 2% year-on-year to Rs 345/bag in FY26 and are projected to increase a further 2-4% in FY27, supported by healthy demand and improved pricing discipline.
- ICRA estimates industry PBITDA/MT will rise to Rs 900-950 in FY26 before moderating to Rs 820-870 per MT in FY27, reflecting anticipated headwinds from fuel and freight cost inflation.
- The industry is entering a major capacity expansion cycle — CRISIL projects 150-160 MT of new capacity between FY25 and FY28 — which is expected to intensify competitive dynamics and require disciplined pricing and efficient cost management.
- Policy tailwinds: the Union Budget 2026-27 allocates a record Rs 12.2 lakh crore to capital expenditure, with Rs 3.09 lakh crore to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, alongside PM Gati Shakti, PMAY-Urban 2.0, AMRUT and Smart Cities, Bharatmala and Sagarmala, and Jal Jeevan Mission.
- Geopolitical tension between the United States and Iran could push crude and gas prices upward; higher diesel and pet-coke prices may exert pressure on operating margins given energy and freight are a significant share of cement production and distribution cost.
- Cost levers management is pulling: renewable energy usage of approximately 33-35%, WHRB captive generation, open-access power procurement through IEX at rates below DISCOM tariffs, biomass and bamboo as alternative fuels, and a long-term Fuel Supply Agreement with Coal India Limited.
- Logistics cost efficiency through e-bidding, PTPK outlier correction and wheeler- and segment-wise freight strategies reduced the weighted average lead distance from 225 km to 221 km and lifted the rail coefficient from 6% to 12%; the first cement barge dispatch via Hatsingimari in August 2025 opened inland waterway corridors.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Priority on organic greenfield expansion in North and Bihar; Maintaining dividend discipline while leveraging balance sheet up to 1.5x limit before raising equity; No M&A mentioned.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY 25-26 was a capacity-addition year. The Company's wholly owned subsidiary Star Cement North East Limited commissioned a 2 MTPA grinding unit in the Cachar area of Silchar district, Assam on 20 February 2026, taking total grinding capacity to 9.7 MTPA (cement capacity of 9.67 MTPA against 6.1 MTPA of clinker capacity). The railway siding at the Silchar grinding unit is progressing at a fast pace and is expected to be operational by Q3 FY27, strengthening logistics efficiency and reducing transportation costs. Star Cement North East Limited has also been declared preferred bidder for the limestone mine at Parewar (SN-IV), District Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, with estimated reserves of 271.38 million tonnes, securing long-term raw material for expansion into new markets. A pipeline of projects is under implementation: a 2 MTPA grinding unit in Bihar, planned as a natural extension of the Siliguri grinding unit and expected to be commissioned by FY28 with the support of government incentives; and two greenfield projects in North India — a 3.3 MTPA clinker unit together with a 2.5 MTPA grinding unit at Nimbol, Rajasthan, and a 2 MTPA grinding unit at Jhajjar, Haryana — both expected to be commissioned by FY28. Management states it is scaling installed cement capacity to 15 MTPA by the end of FY29, consistent with the stated vision of reaching 15 million metric tonnes of manufacturing capacity over the next five years. In the Other Building Materials segment, subsidiary Star Smart Building Solutions Limited commissioned an 800 cubic metre Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (AAC) block plant on 2 June 2025 at Chamata Pathar, Sonapur, adjacent to the existing grinding unit near Guwahati, and the Company extended into construction chemicals including wall putty and entered Ready-Mix Concrete with intent to scale in phases. Earlier milestones in the capacity build include the FY 24-25 commissioning of a 3.3 MTPA clinker line plus an additional 12 MW Waste Heat Recovery System at Lumshnong, the FY 23-24 commissioning of a 2.0 MTPA grinding unit at Sonapur, Guwahati, the FY 22-23 commissioning of a 12.3 MW WHRS at Lumshnong and the FY 20-21 commissioning of a 2.0 MTPA grinding unit at Mohitnagar, Siliguri. Star Cement reports 5 manufacturing facilities: 1 integrated manufacturing unit with WHR, 3 cement grinding units, 1 clinker unit with cement grinding and a 51 MW captive thermal power plant and WHR, and 1 AAC block facility. Debottlenecking of clinker lines and the ramp-up of the expanded Guwahati Grinding Unit and Line-III clinker capacity were the other capacity levers during the year. Of the Company's capex investments in FY 2025-26, 7.73% went to specific technologies improving environmental and social impacts (against 23% in FY 2024-25), covering environmental monitoring equipment, a first aid room and fly ash construction. The rupee quantum of total capital expenditure is not stated in usable form in this bundle.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident on Northeast pricing power and volume growth; Cautious on North India entry emphasizing brand building over volume dumping; Transparent on subsidy headwinds and one-off freight costs; Aggressive on long-term capex vision.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Market leadership in North-East India built over more than two decades of presence, with an approximately 25% trade market share in FY26 and the first cement brand in the region to surpass 5 MTPA of sales in a single financial year.
- Distribution depth — a network of 1,850+ dealers and 11,200+ retailers (RSARs) giving last-mile reach across Eastern and North-Eastern India, reinforced by three digital loyalty platforms (Star Saathi, Star Link, Star Stellar).
- Integrated, cost-efficient manufacturing at Lumshnong with captive limestone reserves, a 51 MW captive thermal power plant and a 24.3 MW Waste Heat Recovery System, and clinker sourced power supplied under a long-term arrangement from wholly owned subsidiary Star Cement Meghalaya Limited.
- Logistics as a competitive advantage in difficult North-East terrain — a dedicated fleet including 274 16-wheelers for clinker movement from Lumshnong to the Guwahati grinding units, weighted average lead distance reduced from 225 km to 221 km and the rail coefficient improved from 6% to 12%.
- Brand equity and premiumisation — Star Weather Shield and Star Dhalai Master raised premium products to about 14% of trade sales in FY 25-26 from about 11% in FY 24-25.
- Energy and cost flexibility — renewable energy usage of approximately 33-35%, open access power procurement through IEX (DAM, RTM and GDAM) at rates below prevailing DISCOM tariffs, and a long-term Fuel Supply Agreement with Coal India Limited.
- Long-term raw material security from captive limestone reserves plus preferred-bidder status for the Parewar (SN-IV) limestone mine in Jaisalmer, Rajasthan with estimated reserves of 271.38 million tonnes.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: 1) Regulatory: Crackdown on illegal coal mining in Meghalaya (management claims minimal impact due to FSA contracts); 2) Competition: New capacity by Dalmia/others in North India could pressure pricing; 3) Execution: Delays in environmental clearances for Rajasthan/Umrangso projects; 4) Subsidy: Structural lower run-rate due to GST changes until new units utilize input credits.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Silchar unit commissioning will initially absorb GST input credits for 7-8 months before becoming eligible for subsidies, delaying subsidy benefit to FY27; Jorhat grinding unit plan dropped in favor of Bihar to better utilize existing clinker; Rajasthan project eligible for 23% CAPEX capital subsidy from state government.

strategy.body:
- Expand beyond the North-East: consolidate leadership in North-East India while extending the footprint into adjacent East India markets (West Bengal, Bihar) and into North India via greenfield projects in Rajasthan and Haryana.

themes.title: Cement demand & pricing recovery
themes.need: Q1FY27 turned cement from a pricing story into a volume-share-plus-fuel-cost story. ULTRACEMCO grew domestic grey volume +13.1% YoY against an estimated ~7-8% industry, delivered its first Rs 5,000cr+ April-June EBITDA (Rs 5,146cr) with EBITDA/ton held above Rs 1,200, and crossed 200.1 MT domestic capacity a year early - but guided Q2FY27 cost UP ~Rs 130-140/ton and pinned the Rs 1,400/ton consolidated target to Q4FY28. The fuel shock, not price, is the swing factor: JKCEMENT's EBITDA/ton fell to Rs 982 from Rs 1,229 YoY despite +19% grey volume, DALBHARAT flagged pet coke 'surged to nearly $160/t' versus a pre-war $110-115, and NUVOCO defended INR 1,079/ton EBITDA only by cutting petcoke from 37% to 27% of fuel mix in a single quarter. Consolidation is visibly compounding (INDIACEM EBITDA/ton Rs 386->400->509->603 across four quarters; DALBHARAT closed Jaypee at Rs 2,850cr EV with Chunar operational and Rewa on trial within 50 days) even as DALBHARAT slipped its 75mt milestone from FY27 to FY28. SHREECEM/RAMCOCEM/JKLAKSHMI/JSWCEMENT/STARCEMENT/BIRLACORPN ride the same volume + consolidation axis.
themes.driver: Q2FY27 is the guided cost trough - ULTRACEMCO ~Rs 130-140/ton, JKCEMENT ~Rs 150/ton and BIRLACORPN Rs 70-80/ton of incremental cost; then fuel-mix agility (NUVOCO's petcoke swing) and whether DALBHARAT's ~Rs 150/t of procurement savings is really 'permanent, not timing'.
